MOSCOW, Russia (CNN)  -- A passenger jet caught fire early Sunday, exploded and crashed into railway tracks in the central Russian city of Perm, killing all 88 people on board. Wreckage from the Aeroflot-Nord Boeing 737, which crashed near Perm, lies across a railway track. The exact cause of the pre-dawn crash is under investigation, but government spokesman Vladimir Markin said "a technical breakdown" was a likely cause. Markin said in televised remarks that the failure of one of the Boeing 737-500's two engines may have caused the plane to come down, The Associated Press reported. Airline officials have said there is no indication of terrorism. "We think it's very doubtful that it was the result of a terrorist attack, because at the scene, there were no traces of explosives as we know for now," said Lev Koshlyakov, Deputy Director General of Aeroflot. It took firefighters more than two hours to extinguish the blazing wreckage. When the sun rose, pieces of the Aeroflot jet were strewn about the railroad tracks. "It slammed in front of my house, and there was a huge flame," an unidentified woman in Perm told Russian state television. "It looked like fireworks." She said the impact of the crash "threw me across my sheets.... Then my daughter ran in from the next room and asked if a war had started." She and other witnesses said they saw the aircraft burning before it came crashing down. "It looked like a comet," she said. The jet was en route to Perm from Moscow when the pilots lost communication with air traffic control just before landing about 3:10 a.m. (2110 GMT), an Aeroflot official said. He described the weather at the time as "mediocre." The public safety minister for the Perm region said investigators were combing a 2.5-mile (4-kilometer) area, including homes and railways.  Watch more about the crash » . "Right now, it's apparent that there was a fire on the plane at one kilometer in the air," Yuri Orlov said. "After that, all contact was cut off -- the plane exploded." The flight data recorder has been recovered and will be analyzed by the International Aviation Commission, Russian Transport Minister Igor Levitin said. The plane carried 82 passengers, including seven children, and a crew of six. At least 21 non-Russians were on board, including passport-holders from Azerbaijan, Germany, France, Italy, Switzerland and Ukraine, said Lev Koshlyakov, Aeroflot's deputy director general. The U.S. Embassy confirmed that no Americans were on board the flight, even though one passenger was listed as a U.S. citizen. It is the second crash in the region involving a Boeing 737 in less than a month. An Iran-bound Boeing 737 with 90 people on board crashed on August 24 just outside the airport in Kyrgyzstan's capital, Bishkek, killing 68. The 737 is a workhorse of the airline industry, with thousands of planes in service. Aeroflot said the one that crashed in Perm was manufactured in 1992 and was operated by its Aeroflot-Nord subsidiary. "This Boeing 737 has all the necessary certificates," Koshlyakov said. "We conduct audits and inspections of all the affiliate companies we work with in the realm of their effectiveness, safety and reliability of the airplanes." Airline safety in Russia and the former Soviet Union is among the worst in the world. Aviation experts say poor maintenance, inadequate pilot training and weak government controls are major factors. But Aeroflot is considered one of the safer airlines in the region. Sunday's crash is the first fatal accident for the airline since 1994, when a Russian pilot handed control of an Airbus to his 15-year-old son. It crashed, killing all 75 people on board. Russia's government has now ordered an inquiry into the latest incident, to find out how another routine flight could have ended in tragedy. The National Transportation Safety Board will send a team of investigators to Perm to look into the incident -- a standard practice when a U.S.-made aircraft crashes. CNN's Kathleen Koch and Michael Sefanov contributed to this report .

**MOSCOW, Russia (CNN)** — A passenger jet burst into flames early Sunday, exploding before crashing onto railway tracks in the central Russian city of Perm and killing all 88 people on board. Debris from the Aeroflot-Nord Boeing 737 lay scattered across the rail line following the pre-dawn tragedy. 

While the precise cause of the crash remains under investigation, government spokesman Vladimir Markin stated that a "technical breakdown" was the probable catalyst. In televised remarks reported by The Associated Press, Markin noted that the failure of one of the Boeing 737-500's two engines might have caused the aircraft to descend. 

Airline officials have dismissed suspicions of foul play. "We think it's very doubtful that it was the result of a terrorist attack, because at the scene, there were no traces of explosives as we know for now," stated Lev Koshlyakov, Deputy Director General of Aeroflot.

Firefighters battled the raging inferno for more than two hours before extinguishing the wreckage. As dawn broke, fragments of the jet were visible, strewn along the railroad tracks. 

"It slammed in front of my house, and there was a huge flame," an unidentified Perm resident told Russian state television. "It looked like fireworks." She recalled that the force of the impact "threw me across my sheets.... Then my daughter ran in from the next room and asked if a war had started." She and other eyewitnesses reported seeing the plane ablaze prior to impact, adding, "It looked like a comet."

The flight was en route from Moscow to Perm when air traffic control lost contact with the pilots at approximately 3:10 a.m. (2110 GMT), moments before its scheduled landing. An Aeroflot official described the weather conditions at the time as "mediocre." 

Yuri Orlov, the public safety minister for the Perm region, stated that investigators were combing a 2.5-mile (4-kilometer) radius encompassing residential areas and railway lines. "Right now, it's apparent that there was a fire on the plane at one kilometer in the air," Orlov observed. "After that, all contact was cut off — the plane exploded."

Russian Transport Minister Igor Levitin confirmed that the flight data recorder had been recovered and would be analyzed by the International Aviation Commission. 

The aircraft was carrying 82 passengers—including seven children—and a crew of six. Koshlyakov noted that at least 21 foreign nationals were among the victims, holding passports from Azerbaijan, France, Germany, Italy, Switzerland, and Ukraine. Although one passenger was initially listed as a U.S. citizen, the U.S. Embassy subsequently confirmed that no Americans were aboard the flight.

This incident marks the region's second fatal crash involving a Boeing 737 in under a month, following an August 24 disaster in which an Iran-bound flight crashed shortly after takeoff near Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, killing 68 of the 90 people aboard. Widely regarded as a workhorse of the global airline industry, thousands of Boeing 737s remain in active service. Aeroflot reported that the aircraft involved in the Perm crash was manufactured in 1992 and operated by its subsidiary, Aeroflot-Nord. 

"This Boeing 737 has all the necessary certificates," Koshlyakov stated. "We conduct audits and inspections of all the affiliate companies we work with in the realm of their effectiveness, safety and reliability of the airplanes."

Aviation safety records across Russia and the former Soviet states are historically among the poorest globally, with experts citing substandard maintenance, insufficient pilot training, and lax regulatory oversight as primary contributors. However, Aeroflot itself is considered one of the safer airlines in the region. Sunday's disaster represents the carrier's first fatal crash since 1994, when a pilot handed control of an Airbus to his 15-year-old son, leading to a crash that killed all 75 people aboard. 

The Russian government has ordered an official inquiry to determine how another routine flight could end in tragedy. Additionally, the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will dispatch a team of investigators to Perm—a standard procedure whenever an American-manufactured aircraft is involved in a crash. 

*CNN's Kathleen Koch and Michael Sefanov contributed to this report.*

At the center of this international coverage has been **CNN**, the world’s first 24-hour news network, which historically played a crucial role in bringing the realities of the Kremlin and the Russian people to a global audience.

The relationship between the network and the host nation dates back to the late Cold War era. When CNN established its bureau in Moscow, it opened a direct channel of real-time information from behind the Iron Curtain. During the tumultuous early 1990s, CNN’s live broadcasts from Red Square and outside the White House in Moscow captured history in the making—from the collapse of the Soviet Union to the chaotic birth of the modern Russian Federation. For millions of viewers worldwide, the network's correspondents became the primary translators of Russia’s complex political evolution.

Over the years, reporting from Moscow required navigating an increasingly delicate balance. As the political climate in Russia shifted under President Vladimir Putin, the environment for foreign journalists grew progressively challenging. CNN continued to cover major national stories—ranging from domestic political crackdowns and economic shifts to Russia’s expanding global influence and foreign interventions—often facing pushback from state authorities regarding its editorial perspective.

A critical turning point occurred in March 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In response to sweeping new Russian legislation that criminalized independent journalism and restricted narrative control over the conflict, CNN made the difficult decision to suspend its broadcasting and on-the-ground reporting operations inside Russia. The safety of its journalists became paramount under laws that threatened long prison sentences for reporting that contradicted the government's official stance.

The suspension of CNN’s physical presence in Moscow marked the end of an era of unprecedented journalistic access. Today, while reporting *from* Russia has become severely limited, the country remains a focal point of CNN’s international news coverage. **Headline:** Passenger Jet Crashes in Russia's Urals, All 88 Onboard Killed  
**Byline:** Matthew Chance, CNN Moscow Bureau  
**Dateline:** MOSCOW, Russia — September 14, 2008  

A Boeing 737 passenger jet carrying 88 people crashed early Sunday morning on the outskirts of the Ural Mountains city of Perm, killing everyone on board, according to Russian emergency officials. 

Flight SU821, operated by regional carrier Aeroflot-Nord on behalf of Russia's flag carrier Aeroflot, was on its final approach to Perm International Airport after a two-hour flight from Moscow's Sheremetyevo Airport. 

According to the Russian Emergency Situations Ministry (EMERCOM), air traffic control lost contact with the aircraft at approximately 3:15 a.m. local time (5:15 p.m. ET Saturday) at an altitude of roughly 1,800 feet. The plane slammed into a ravine adjacent to a residential district, narrowly missing nearby apartment blocks but crashing onto a section of the Trans-Siberian Railway, destroying hundreds of yards of track.

Emergency workers at the scene confirmed that all 82 passengers—including seven children—and six crew members perished in the fiery crash. 

"All 88 people aboard were killed instantly. There are no survivors," said EMERCOM spokesman Irina Andrianova. She added that while no ground casualties were reported, the debris field was spread over several square kilometers.

Among the victims was Gen. Gennady Troshev, a prominent former military commander who led Russian forces in the Second Chechen War and later served as an adviser to former President Vladimir Putin.

### Night of Terror in Perm

Residents of the industrial city, located some 750 miles east of Moscow, described scenes of horror as the plane came down during low cloud cover and rain.

"It was like a bright fireball falling right out of the sky," said Evgeny, a local resident whose apartment building sits less than half a mile from the crash site. "The noise was terrifying—it sounded like a roaring missile. Then came a massive explosion that shook our whole building and blew open our windows. We looked out and saw a wall of flame near the railroad tracks."

Another witness, Yelena, told Russian television that the aircraft appeared to be out of control before impact. 

"There was no sound of the engine revving down—just a sudden, terrifying whistle and a burst of light," she said. "It is a miracle it did not land directly on our homes. It missed the apartment towers by just a few hundred yards."

### Official Response and Investigation

The Interstate Aviation Committee (MAK), Russia’s civil aviation investigating body, has launched a full criminal investigation. Transport Minister Igor Levitin and a team of federal investigators have flown to the site, where search crews have already recovered both the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder—the "black boxes"—from the scorched debris.

Aeroflot officials expressed condolences and promised full financial compensation to the families of the victims, while attempting to clarify the relationship with its subsidiary.

"We are deeply saddened by this tragic event and share the grief of the victims' families," Lev Koshlyakov, a spokesman for Aeroflot, told CNN in Moscow. "Aeroflot-Nord operated this flight using its own aircraft and crew. However, Aeroflot is taking full responsibility for assisting the families and supporting the official investigation."

Koshlyakov noted that the pilot was experienced and that the Boeing 737-500, which had been leased from a foreign firm, was fully airworthy prior to takeoff.

Russian Transport Ministry officials stated that it was too early to determine the cause of the crash, though preliminary reports suggest technical failure or engine trouble, combined with poor weather conditions during descent, are being primary areas of focus. Terrorism has been preliminarily ruled out.

### Shadow Over Russian Aviation Safety

Sunday's disaster re-opens a painful debate regarding Russia's air safety record, which has come under intense scrutiny in recent years.

While the 1990s saw a wave of crashes involving aging Soviet-era aircraft, the mid-2000s have seen a series of fatal accidents that raised questions about training, maintenance, and oversight—even as Russian airlines rapidly modernize their fleets with foreign-built jets like Boeing and Airbus.

In 2006 alone, Russia suffered three major airline disasters: an S7 Airlines Airbus A310 crash in Irkutsk that killed 125 people, a Pulkovo Aviation Enterprise Tu-154 crash in Ukraine that killed 170, and an Armavia crash into the Black Sea that claimed 113 lives. 

Those tragedies prompted the Kremlin to push for stricter regulatory oversight and the phase-out of older Soviet aircraft models. However, experts point out that rapid growth in Russia's commercial aviation sector has put immense pressure on pilot training programs and air traffic control infrastructure.

"This crash is a devastating blow," said an aviation analyst based in Moscow who requested anonymity. "The Boeing 737 is considered the workhorse of global aviation. If a modern Western aircraft operated under the banner of the country’s flag carrier can suffer a catastrophe like this, it indicates systemic issues that go far beyond just the age of the planes."

As rain continues to fall over Perm, rescue crews are working through the smoldering wreckage to recover human remains and clear the damaged Trans-Siberian rail lines. Prime Minister Vladimir Putin has ordered a state commission to be formed to oversee the crash response and provide aid to the victims' families.

**SPECIAL INVESTIGATIVE REPORT: The Crash of Aeroflot-Nord Flight 821**

**MOSCOW / PERM, Russia** — In the early hours of September 14, 2008, Aeroflot-Nord Flight 821, a Boeing 737-500 operating on behalf of Russia’s flag carrier Aeroflot, crashed during its final approach to Perm International Airport. The airliner plunged into a ravine adjacent to the Trans-Siberian Railway, just meters from a densely populated residential area. 

All 88 people on board—82 passengers and 6 crew members—were killed instantly. 

Subsequent investigations by Russia’s Interstate Aviation Committee (MAK) revealed a tragic chain of systemic failures, spatial disorientation, poor CRM (Crew Resource Management), and pilot impairment, making it one of the deadliest aviation disasters involving a Boeing 737 in Russian history.

---

### **The Incident: Fatal Descent in the Dark**

Flight 821 departed Moscow’s Sheremetyevo Airport at 1:12 a.m. local time, bound for the Ural mountain city of Perm. The flight proceeded normally until the aircraft reached the final descent phase into Perm under dark, overcast skies with rain and a low cloud ceiling (around 300 meters).

At 5:09 a.m., air traffic control (ATC) instructed the flight crew to begin a turn to align with the runway's instrument landing system (ILS). However, the aircraft began executing maneuvers that left controllers baffled:

* Instead of descending, the plane began climbing.
* When instructed to turn right, the plane turned left, and vice versa.
* ATC repeatedly warned the crew that they were off course and climbing rather than descending.

In the final radio exchange, controller Irek Birbov asked the crew if everything was normal aboard the aircraft. Captain Rodion Medvedev responded in an agitated tone, *"Affirmative."* Seconds later, the controller warned the aircraft that it was in a steep left bank. The final, desperate cry from the cockpit recorder captured the First Officer screaming, *"What are we doing?!"* before the transmission cut off at 5:13 a.m.

The Boeing 737 rolled completely inverted, entering an almost vertical dive, and slammed into the ground at a speed exceeding 470 km/h (290 mph).

---

### **Eyewitness Accounts: "A Burning Meteor"**

The crash occurred in the industrial suburb of Perm, ripping through a railway track and damaging power lines. Miraculously, despite hitting a populated urban area, no one on the ground was killed.

* **Svetlana Kouznetsova, local resident:**  
  *"I was woken up by a deafening roar that shook the entire house. It sounded like a rocket landing in the backyard. I looked out the window and saw a bright orange flash that turned the night into day. Debris was raining down, and the smell of aviation fuel was overwhelming."*

* **Sergei Yushkov, eyewitness:**  
  *"The plane was coming down at a terrible angle. It looked like a burning meteor cutting through the cloud layer. It didn't glide; it seemed to fall nose-first. There was a massive explosion when it hit the ravine near the tracks."*

* **Irek Birbov, Air Traffic Controller on duty:**  
  *In interviews following the crash, Birbov noted that the pilot’s responses sounded erratic and unresponsive to clear vectors. "He acted contrary to instructions. I told him to turn right; he turned left. He was completely out of control of his trajectory, yet insisted everything was fine."*

First responders arriving at the scene described a site of total devastation. The aircraft was obliterated into thousands of small fragments scattered along a section of the Trans-Siberian Railway, severing communications and blocking train traffic along the vital artery for several days.

---

### **Casualties Breakdown**

There were no survivors. The 88 victims comprised 82 passengers (including 7 children) and 6 crew members.

#### **Demographics & Nationalities:**
While the majority of the victims were Russian citizens, foreign nationals from seven other countries were aboard:
* **Russia:** 68 (including 6 crew members)
* **Azerbaijan:** 9
* **Ukraine:** 5
* **France:** 1
* **Switzerland:** 1
* **Latvia:** 1
* **Germany:** 1
* **Uzbekistan:** 1
* **Turkey:** 1

#### **Notable Passengers:**
Among the dead was **General Gennady Troshev**, a high-ranking Russian military commander who had previously served as the commander of federal forces in the Chechen Wars and was serving as an advisor to Russian President Dmitry Medvedev at the time of the crash. A delegation from the Russian Sambo Federation was also on board.

---

### **The Investigation and Official Findings**

The Interstate Aviation Committee (MAK), assisted by the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and Boeing, conducted an exhaustive investigation using recovered Black Boxes (Flight Data Recorder and Cockpit Voice Recorder).

The final report, released in February 2009, cited **loss of control due to spatial disorientation** as the primary cause of the crash, compounded by severe pilot error and inadequate training.

#### **Key Investigative Findings:**

1. **Spatial Disorientation & Attitude Indicator Confusion:**
   The captain experienced a severe case of spatial disorientation (somatogravic illusion) while flying manually through dense clouds at night. Crucially, the pilots had transitioned from Soviet-built aircraft (An-24, Tu-134) to Western aircraft (Boeing 737). 
   * **Russian/Soviet Horizon Indicators (Attitude Indicators):** Feature a fixed airplane symbol with a moving sky/ground background.
   * **Western Horizon Indicators:** Feature a moving airplane symbol against a fixed horizon.
   Under extreme stress and darkness, Captain Medvedev confused the horizon indications. When he thought the plane was banking right, he applied left-roll control inputs, unintentionally pushing the plane into an inverted, irreversible roll.

2. **Pilot Impairment (Alcohol):**
   Post-mortem toxicological analysis revealed the presence of alcohol in the tissue of Captain Rodion Medvedev. The CVR recorded the captain slurring his words and acting erratically during the approach, while the First Officer, Rustam Allaberdin—who was far less experienced—failed to intervene or take control of the aircraft.

3. **Inadequate Training and Fatigue:**
   Neither pilot had completed sufficient simulator training for handling spatial disorientation or recovery from unusual flight attitudes in Western aircraft. Furthermore, the crew had been subjected to irregular sleep cycles and high fatigue levels in the days leading up to the flight.

4. **Engine Asymmetry (Unbalanced Thrust):**
   A minor technical defect present on the aircraft—a thrust asymmetry caused by an uncalibrated autothrottle system—forced the pilots to manage unbalanced engines manually. This added to their workload during a critical, high-stress phase of flight.

---

### **Aftermath and Industry Impact**

The crash of Flight 821 sent shockwaves through Russia's aviation industry and led to swift administrative consequences:

* **Corporate Rebranding:** Aeroflot immediately severed ties with its subsidiary's branding. Aeroflot-Nord was prohibited from using the Aeroflot brand name and was subsequently rebranded as **Nordavia** (later becoming Smartavia).
* **Training Reforms:** Rosaviatsia (Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency) mandated stricter retraining programs for pilots transitioning from Soviet-era avionics to Western glass cockpits, focusing heavily on spatial orientation awareness.
* **Pre-Flight Medical Checks:** The disaster prompted a complete overhaul and strict enforcement of pre-flight medical screenings to ensure zero tolerance for alcohol or substance impairment among flight crews across all Russian carriers.

A memorial chapel and monument were later erected near the crash site in Perm, bearing the names of all 88 victims of Flight 821.

Over the past decade, Aeroflot has aggressively worked to overhaul its image, modernizing its fleet with Western-built Boeing and Airbus aircraft and striving to meet international safety standards. Aeroflot-Nord, a regional subsidiary operating out of northern Russia, utilized the Boeing 737-500 involved in Sunday's accident. 

Despite recent industry improvements across the country, safety experts point out that regional operations in Russia continue to face scrutiny regarding maintenance practices and training standards. 

Teams from Russia’s Ministry of Emergency Situations and the Interstate Aviation Committee (MAK) remain at the crash site searching for the aircraft’s flight data recorders, commonly known as the black boxes, to determine the exact cause of the tragedy.

**ALL 88 ABOARD KILLED AS PASSENGER JET CRASHES NEAR RUSSIAN CITY OF PERM**

**PERM, Russia** — A Boeing 737 passenger airliner carrying 88 people crashed early Sunday morning on its final approach to the Ural mountain city of Perm, killing everyone on board in one of Russia’s worst aviation disasters in recent years. 

Aeroflot Flight 821, operated by regional subsidiary Aeroflot-Nord, was en route from Moscow’s Sheremetyevo Airport to Perm when it lost contact with air traffic controllers at approximately 5:10 a.m. local time (23:10 GMT Saturday). The aircraft plunged into a ravine just yards from a residential area, slamming directly onto a section of the Trans-Siberian Railway.

Emergency services confirmed that all 82 passengers—including seven children and seven foreign nationals—and six crew members perished instantly upon impact. Remarkably, despite the plane exploding into flames near high-rise apartment buildings, no casualties were reported on the ground. 

"The plane went down in a steep dive, exploded, and was almost completely destroyed," said a spokesperson for the Russian Emergencies Ministry. "Search crews have cleared the immediate site, but there are no survivors."

The impact damaged a track section of the Trans-Siberian Railway, severing rail traffic between Perm and Yekaterinburg and disrupting power lines in the surrounding district. Firefighters worked for hours to douse the flames sparked by burning jet fuel.

### High-Profile Victim Among the Dead

Officials confirmed that among the passengers killed was Gen. Gennady Troshev, a prominent former military commander who led Russian forces during the Second Chechen War and served as an advisor to the Russian president. His death was later confirmed by the Ministry of Defense. 

The passenger list also included citizens from the United States, France, Germany, Turkey, Italy, Switzerland, and Azerbaijan, according to Aeroflot representatives.

### Flight Controllers Describe Erratic Maneuvers

Air traffic controllers at Perm Airport reported that the aircraft was attempting its landing approach under low clouds and rain when trouble began. 

According to flight control logs, after being instructed to turn left for alignment with the runway, the aircraft made an uncommanded turn to the right and began to climb rather than descend. When air traffic control questioned the maneuver, the pilot radioed back that the system was operating normally, yet the aircraft continued to behave erratically.

Seconds later, the Boeing 737 rolled completely upside down, entered a steep vertical dive, and struck the ground at high speed. 

### Investigation Points to Disorientation, Training Deficits, and Alcohol

Investigators from Russia’s Interstate Aviation Committee (IAC), alongside representatives from the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and Boeing, recovered both the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder from the wreckage. 

Findings released by safety regulators reveal a catastrophic combination of spatial disorientation, inadequate pilot training, and crew impairment:

* **Spatial Disorientation:** Clouds and pitch-black conditions deprived the flight crew of visual reference points. Investigators determined that Captain Rodion Medvedev suffered severe spatial disorientation, misinterpreting the position of the aircraft relative to the horizon.
* **Instrument Differences:** The crew lacked sufficient training on Western-style "attitude indicators" (artificial horizons), which operate differently from the Soviet-designed indicators the pilots were accustomed to flying. This led the captain to input wrong flight commands while attempting to level the plane.
* **Pilot Impairment:** Forensic analysis confirmed the presence of alcohol in the captain's system prior to the flight, severely impairing his judgment and motor skills during the critical phase of landing.
* **Crew Miscommunication:** Cockpit voice recordings revealed poor crew resource management. The first officer failed to intervene or take effective control of the aircraft as the captain grew increasingly disoriented.
* **Mechanical Factor:** A known, uncorrected imbalance in engine thrust (autothrottle split) forced the pilots to manually manage engine output, further increasing their workload during the fatal approach.

### Aftermath and Repercussions

Russian President Dmitry Medvedev was briefed on the crash and ordered the creation of a special government commission to assist the victims' families and investigate the root causes of the disaster.

In the immediate wake of the crash, national carrier Aeroflot moved to distance itself from its subsidiary. Aeroflot announced that it would revoke the use of its brand name from Aeroflot-Nord and completely revamp training procedures for pilots transitioning from Soviet-era aircraft to modern Western fleets.

Aeroflot has announced it will pay up to 2 million rubles ($78,000 USD) in compensation to the families of each victim, as recovery teams continue the grim task of identifying human remains at the crash site using DNA matching.
